Case name: ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. v. Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether the supervisory court at the seat can finish adjudicating an already-heard Section 9 application after the arbitral tribunal is constituted.
Holding in one line: The bar under Section 9(3) does not oust the jurisdiction of the seat court to pronounce orders on a Section 9 petition already heard and reserved.
Case explanation: Disputes arose under a cargo handling agreement where the seat court had heard extensive Section 9 interim protection arguments before the tribunal was formally constituted. The Supreme Court clarified that 'entertain' in Section 9(3) means taking up for consideration; once the supervisory court at the seat has applied its mind and reserved orders, it need not relegate parties to Section 17.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd. (2020) 4 SCC 234

Case name: State of Chhattisgarh v. Sal Udyog Private Limited
Issue in one line: Whether patent illegality going to the root of the award can be raised before the supervisory seat court under Section 37 even if omitted in Section 34 pleadings.
Holding in one line: Supervisory courts at the arbitral seat retain jurisdiction to examine patent illegality apparent on the face of the award under Section 34(2A).
Case explanation: In a Sal seed supply contract with the State of Chhattisgarh, the arbitral tribunal awarded refund of supervision charges contrary to express contractual clauses. The 3-Judge Bench held that ignoring binding contract terms constitutes 'patent illegality' under Section 34(2A), and the supervisory court at the seat is empowered to correct it even if raised first in a Section 37 appeal.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI (2019) 15 SCC 131

Case name: AP Education & Welfare Infrastructure Dev. Corp. v. M/s Mape Connoisseurs Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether the High Court exercising jurisdiction over the designated seat rightly appointed the arbitrator despite administrative actions elsewhere.
Holding in one line: The High Court having territorial jurisdiction over the contractually designated seat possesses exclusive competence under Section 11(6).
Case explanation: The State Infrastructure Corporation challenged the High Court's appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11(6) on territorial grounds. The Supreme Court dismissed the SLP, affirming that once the seat of arbitration is anchored within a High Court's territory, that High Court exercises exclusive referral competence.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Indus Mobile Distribution Pvt. Ltd. v. Datawind Innovations (2017) 7 SCC 678

Case name: Intercontinental Hotels Group (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Waterline Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether stamp duty sufficiency disputes can stall appointment of an arbitrator at the designated seat in an international commercial arbitration.
Holding in one line: Once the arbitration clause fixing the seat is prima facie valid, the supervisory court must appoint the tribunal and leave curable stamp issues to the tribunal.
Case explanation: In an India-seated hotel management dispute, the respondent resisted Section 11(6) appointment alleging insufficient stamp duty on the underlying contract. The 3-Judge Bench held that where stamp duty has been paid and only its adequacy is contested, the supervisory court at the seat should not delay constituting the tribunal.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (2021) 2 SCC 1

Case name: Ravi Ranjan Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. Aditya Kumar Chatterjee
Issue in one line: Whether naming Kolkata strictly as a convenient place for sittings confers Section 11(6) jurisdiction on the Calcutta High Court when property and cause of action lie in Muzaffarpur.
Holding in one line: A clause specifying a place merely for arbitral sittings without exclusive jurisdiction indicia is a geographical venue, not a juridical seat; Calcutta HC lacked jurisdiction.
Case explanation: A development agreement for property in Muzaffarpur, Bihar stated that 'sitting of the arbitral tribunal shall be at Kolkata.' The Supreme Court set aside the Calcutta High Court's appointment order, ruling that 'sitting at Kolkata' merely indicated a convenient physical venue under Section 20(3), not a juridical seat under Section 20(1).
Precedent chiefly relied on: Mankastu Impex Pvt. Ltd. v. Airvisual Ltd. (2020) 5 SCC 399

Case name: Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Discovery Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: How supervisory courts at the seat must evaluate non-signatory joinder under the group of companies doctrine.
Holding in one line: Laid down the five-factor test (mutual intent, composite transaction, common performance) for binding non-signatories within the seat's lex arbitri.
Case explanation: ONGC sought to bind a non-signatory group company in an India-seated arbitration. The 3-Judge Bench set aside the interim award that had prematurely deleted the non-signatory, formulating the classic 5-factor test (mutual intention, relationship, composite nature, common performance) and referring the overarching doctrinal validity to a 5-Judge Constitution Bench.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Chloro Controls India Pvt. Ltd. v. Severn Trent Water Purification Inc. (2013) 1 SCC 641

Case name: Swadesh Kumar Agarwal v. Dinesh Kumar Agarwal
Issue in one line: Whether termination of an arbitrator's mandate on de jure/de facto inability lies under Section 11(6) before the High Court or Section 14(2) before the Principal Civil Court of the seat.
Holding in one line: Disputes over termination of mandate under Section 14(2) must be filed exclusively before the 'Court' under Section 2(1)(e) at the arbitral seat, not via Section 11(6).
Case explanation: A party directly approached the High Court under Section 11(6) to terminate the mandate of an existing sole arbitrator for alleged unreasonable delay. The Supreme Court held that a controversy over whether an arbitrator's mandate stands terminated under Section 14(1)(a) must be adjudicated exclusively by the Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction at the seat under Section 14(2) read with Section 2(1)(e).
Precedent chiefly relied on: SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. (2005) 8 SCC 618

Case name: BBR (India) Private Limited v. S.P. Singla Constructions Private Limited
Issue in one line: Whether a substitute arbitrator holding hearings in Delhi shifts the juridical seat earlier fixed at Panchkula by the first arbitrator under Section 20(2).
Holding in one line: Once the jurisdictional seat is fixed at Panchkula under Section 20(2), subsequent sittings in Delhi by a successor arbitrator are merely convenient venues and cannot shift the seat.
Case explanation: The contract was silent on the seat, so the initial arbitrator fixed Panchkula, Haryana as the seat under Section 20(2). After he recused, the substitute arbitrator held hearings and pronounced the award in Delhi. The Supreme Court held that once the seat is determined under Section 20(2), a successor arbitrator changing the physical venue to Delhi without mutual party consent does not shift Section 34 supervisory jurisdiction away from Panchkula.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd. (2020) 4 SCC 234

Case name: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. v. IVRCL AMR Joint Venture
Issue in one line: Whether a departmental circular providing for redressal without reference to arbitration or a designated seat constitutes a valid arbitration agreement.
Holding in one line: Absent clear intent to refer disputes to binding arbitration at an agreed forum, the High Court lacked Section 11(6) jurisdiction to appoint an arbitrator.
Case explanation: Clause 15 of the contract was titled 'Settlement of Disputes/Arbitration' but only provided for internal settlement by an Engineer-in-Charge, failing which parties were to approach civil courts. The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's Section 11 order, ruling that mere use of the word 'Arbitration' in a heading does not confer arbitral jurisdiction without a binding agreement under Section 7.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Jagdish Chander v. Ramesh Chander (2007) 5 SCC 719

Case name: Continental India Private Limited v. General Manager Northern Railway
Issue in one line: Whether the High Court at the seat erred in directing constitution of a Railway GCC panel when the main contract contained no reference to the GCC and the respondent forfeited its right.
Holding in one line: Where the respondent failed to appoint an arbitrator within 30 days of invocation and the GCC was inapplicable, the supervisory court must appoint an independent sole arbitrator.
Case explanation: After Northern Railway failed to appoint an arbitrator upon invocation of Clause 32, the Allahabad High Court directed constitution of a panel under the 2020 Railway GCC. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, noting that the GCC was never incorporated into the main agreement and appointed Former Supreme Court Justice R. Banumathi as sole arbitrator.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Deep Trading Company v. Indian Oil Corporation (2013) 4 SCC 35

Case name: Jaycee Housing Pvt. Ltd. v. Registrar (General), Orissa High Court
Main provision: Section 2(1)(e), Section 20 & Commercial Courts Act Sec. 10
Issue in one line: Whether the State Government notification conferring Section 34 jurisdiction on Commercial Courts subordinate to the Principal District Judge violates Section 2(1)(e).
Holding in one line: Section 2(1)(e) of the Arbitration Act yields to the special mechanism of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 for commercial arbitration petitions at the seat.
Case explanation: Petitioners challenged an Odisha notification designating the Court of the Civil Judge (Senior Division) as a Commercial Court competent to hear Section 9, 14, and 34 applications at the seat. The Supreme Court upheld the notification, holding that Sections 10 and 15 of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 override the general definition of 'Court' in Section 2(1)(e) for commercial disputes of specified value.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Kandla Export Corporation v. OCI Corporation (2018) 14 SCC 715

Case name: Tata Sons Pvt. Ltd. v. Siva Industries and Holdings Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether the 12-month statutory time limit and Section 29A supervisory court extension regime apply to India-seated international commercial arbitrations.
Holding in one line: Following the 2019 Amendment, India-seated international commercial arbitrations are excluded from the mandatory 12-month timeline under Section 29A(1).
Case explanation: In an India-seated international commercial arbitration involving a foreign resident party, Tata Sons sought clarification on whether the sole arbitrator's mandate required judicial extension under Section 29A. The 3-Judge Bench headed by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud ruled that the 2019 Amendment to Section 29A(1) is remedial/procedural and relieves India-seated ICAs from mandatory 12-month judicial extension applications.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BCCI v. Kochi Cricket Pvt. Ltd. (2018) 6 SCC 287

Case name: NTPC Ltd. v. SPML Infra Ltd.
Issue in one line: Scope of the 'Eye of the Needle' inquiry by the High Court of the arbitral seat when a claim is discharged by accord and satisfaction.
Holding in one line: The referral court at the seat must decline Section 11(6) reference where the underlying contract is demonstrably extinguished by full and final settlement.
Case explanation: After SPML Infra executed a settlement agreement and received release of bank guarantees, it repudiated the settlement and moved the Delhi High Court (the seat court) under Section 11(6). Applying the 'Eye of the Needle' test (later narrowed by Krish Spinning in 2024), the 2-Judge Bench set aside the referral, finding the claim ex-facie deadwood.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (2021) 2 SCC 1

Case name: Gujarat Composite Limited v. A Infrastructure Limited
Issue in one line: Whether a composite civil suit involving non-signatories and relief beyond the seated arbitration agreement can be bifurcated under Section 8.
Holding in one line: Where causes of action and non-signatory parties cannot be severed from the seated arbitration clause, civil jurisdiction is not ousted under Section 8.
Case explanation: A licensing dispute involved tripartite transactions, a bank, and recovery of possession against entities not party to the original arbitration agreement. The Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of the Section 8 application, holding that a civil suit cannot be bifurcated where the reliefs and parties fall substantially outside the seated arbitration agreement.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Sukanya Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Jayesh H. Pandya (2003) 5 SCC 531

Case name: Glock Asia-Pacific Limited v. Union of India
Issue in one line: Whether a tender clause allowing the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs to appoint a Ministry Law Officer in a Delhi-seated arbitration violates Section 12(5).
Holding in one line: Unilateral appointment of a serving government officer in a Delhi-seated ICA violates Section 12(5) and the Seventh Schedule; Supreme Court appointed an independent sole arbitrator.
Case explanation: In a global tender for pistol supply seated in New Delhi, the Union of India contended that contracts expressed in the President's name under Article 299 were immune from Section 12(5) neutrality bars. A 3-Judge Bench rejected the plea and appointed a retired Supreme Court Judge as sole arbitrator at the Delhi seat.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd. (2020) 20 SCC 760

Case name: Cox and Kings Ltd. v. SAP India Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Validity of the 'Group of Companies' doctrine under Indian arbitration law when the seat of arbitration is in India.
Holding in one line: Upheld the Group of Companies doctrine grounded in Section 2(1)(h) and Section 7; supervisory courts at the seat do only a prima facie check, leaving final joinder to the tribunal.
Case explanation: Resolving the reference from ONGC v. Discovery Enterprises, a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that non-signatory corporate affiliates can be bound to an India-seated arbitration agreement if mutual conduct demonstrates intent to be bound. Crucially, at the Section 8/11 stage, the supervisory seat court must leave the complex factual determination of joinder to the arbitral tribunal under Section 16.
Precedent chiefly relied on: ONGC Ltd. v. Discovery Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (2022) 8 SCC 42

Case name: M/s Arif Azim Co. Ltd. v. M/s Aptech Ltd.
Issue in one line: Limitation framework for invoking Section 11(6) before the supervisory court of an India-seated international commercial arbitration.
Holding in one line: Established the two-prong limitation test (petition timeliness and deadwood claim test) for India-seated arbitrations and appointed a sole arbitrator.
Case explanation: A Kabul-based franchisee invoked an India-seated arbitration clause against Aptech Ltd. in Mumbai. Justice J.B. Pardiwala's 3-Judge Bench laid down the authoritative two-step inquiry for supervisory courts at the seat: (1) whether the Section 11(6) petition was filed within 3 years of refusal to appoint, and (2) whether the underlying substantive claim was already time-barred on the date of the Section 21 notice.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BSNL v. Nortel Networks India Pvt. Ltd. (2021) 5 SCC 738

Case name: Chief Engineer (NH) PWD (Roads) v. M/s BSC & C and C JV
Citation or case number: SLP (C) No. 10544 of 2024 | 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1801
Issue in one line: Whether power to extend the arbitral mandate under Section 29A(4) vests in the Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction at the seat or exclusively the High Court.
Holding in one line: Unless the High Court possesses ordinary original civil jurisdiction over the seat, Section 29A(4) jurisdiction vests in the Principal Civil Court at the arbitral seat.
Case explanation: Resolving a major split among High Courts, the Supreme Court affirmed the Meghalaya High Court's ruling that 'Court' in Section 29A(4) must be read strictly in accordance with Section 2(1)(e). Where the High Court lacks ordinary original civil jurisdiction over the seat, Section 29A applications lie before the Principal Civil/Commercial Court at the seat.
Precedent chiefly relied on: State of West Bengal v. Associated Contractors (2015) 1 SCC 32

Case name: SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Krish Spinning
Issue in one line: Whether the referral court at the arbitral seat can conduct a mini-trial on 'accord and satisfaction' at the Section 11(6) stage.
Holding in one line: Overruled the broad 'Eye of the Needle' inquiry; the referral court at the seat is strictly restricted to verifying the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement under Section 11(6A).
Case explanation: Following the 7-Judge Stamp Act Constitution Bench, a 3-Judge Bench in Krish Spinning held that earlier decisions like NTPC v. SPML Infra allowing referral courts at the seat to adjudicate 'accord and satisfaction' or discharge by settlement encroached upon the arbitral tribunal's exclusive competence under Section 16.
Precedent chiefly relied on: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements and Stamp Act (2023 INSC 1066)

Case name: Ajay Madhusudan Patel v. Jyotrindra S. Patel
Issue in one line: Joinder of a non-signatory corporate group entity in a domestic seated arbitration based on active participation in contract performance.
Holding in one line: Applied Cox & Kings to refer both signatory and prima facie bound non-signatory parties to the seated arbitral tribunal.
Case explanation: In a family business division involving multiple corporate entities (the SRG Group), a non-signatory group company resisted joinder in the seated arbitration. The 3-Judge Bench held that since the non-signatory's rights and obligations were intertwined in the family arrangement, it should be referred to the tribunal, which will finally decide joinder under Section 16.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Cox and Kings Ltd. v. SAP India Pvt. Ltd. (2024) 4 SCC 1

Case name: M/s Arif Azim Co. Ltd. v. M/s Micromax Informatics FZE
Issue in one line: Whether designating Dubai, UAE as the venue alongside UAE governing law fixes the juridical seat outside India and ousts Supreme Court Section 11(6) jurisdiction.
Holding in one line: Applying the Shashoua principle, designating Dubai as venue coupled with UAE curial/substantive law establishes Dubai as the juridical seat, excluding Part I jurisdiction of Indian courts.
Case explanation: A distribution agreement designated 'Dubai, UAE' as the venue of arbitration and subjected the contract to UAE law and Dubai courts. Dismissing the Section 11(6) petition, the 3-Judge Bench reaffirmed that under the BALCO territoriality principle and BGS SGS Soma, a designated foreign venue without contrary indicia is the juridical seat, barring Part I applications in India.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BALCO v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services Inc. (2012) 9 SCC 552

Case name: Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. M/s ECI SPIC SMO MCML (JV)
Issue in one line: Constitutional and statutory validity of unilateral arbitrator appointment clauses and curated PSU panels in India-seated arbitrations.
Holding in one line: Unilateral appointment clauses and mandatory selection from a narrow PSU-curated panel violate equal treatment under Section 18 and Article 14 across all India-seated arbitrations.
Case explanation: Overruling the 2020 3-Judge CORE decision, a 5-Judge Constitution Bench held that in all India-seated arbitrations governed by Part I, a party with a financial interest in the dispute cannot unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator or compel the counterparty to choose from a curated panel of retired PSU officers.
Precedent chiefly relied on: TRF Ltd. v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd. (2017) 8 SCC 377

Case name: Alpha Residents Welfare Association v. M/s Alpha Corp Development Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether an exclusive forum selection clause can override statutory territorial jurisdiction over immovable housing project disputes.
Holding in one line: The exclusive forum doctrine under Swastik Gases cannot confer jurisdiction on a court where statutory housing/property law mandates local situs jurisdiction.
Case explanation: Residents of a housing township in Karnal filed a suit in Karnal, which was rejected on the strength of Clause 23 granting exclusive jurisdiction to New Delhi courts. The Supreme Court reversed, distinguishing Swastik Gases and holding that where immovable property and statutory local apartment laws are situated in Karnal, parties cannot oust the situs court via a boilerplate Delhi forum clause.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Swastik Gases Pvt. Ltd. v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (2013) 9 SCC 32

Case name: Disortho S.A.S. v. Meril Life Sciences Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether a clause designating Bogota for conciliation/arbitration proceedings displaces Indian supervisory jurisdiction when Indian law governs the contract and Gujarat courts hold jurisdiction.
Holding in one line: Where Indian law governs the contract and Indian courts retain supervisory jurisdiction, Bogota is merely a physical hearing venue; India remains the juridical seat.
Case explanation: A Colombian distributor and an Indian medical device company signed an agreement governed by Indian law and conferring jurisdiction on courts in Gujarat, India, while another clause stated arbitration would take place in Bogota under ICC rules. Applying the 3-stage Enka v. Chubb / Enercon test, the 3-Judge Bench held that Bogota was only a convenient physical venue and appointed a sole arbitrator under Section 11(6) in India.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Enercon (India) Ltd. v. Enercon GmbH (2014) 5 SCC 1

Case name: S.P. Singla Constructions Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Himachal Pradesh
Issue in one line: Whether Section 42 and seat exclusivity principles apply when the underlying dispute resolution clause is a non-binding departmental adjudication clause.
Holding in one line: Section 42 and juridical seat exclusivity apply strictly to valid arbitration agreements under Section 7 and are inapplicable to non-arbitral departmental clauses.
Case explanation: The contractor sought to invoke Section 42 supervisory exclusivity on the basis of prior filings under a works contract clause. The Supreme Court held that territorial sequestration under Section 42 is triggered only by a valid Section 7 arbitration agreement at the designated seat.
Precedent chiefly relied on: State of West Bengal v. Associated Contractors (2015) 1 SCC 32

Case name: Balaji Steel Trade v. Fludor Benin S.A.
Issue in one line: Whether an Indian court can entertain a Section 11(6) petition when the principal contract expressly designates Benin, West Africa as the place of arbitration and Benin law as lex arbitri.
Holding in one line: Express designation of Benin as the arbitral seat and Benin law as curial law triggers the BALCO territoriality bar, excluding Part I of the 1996 Act.
Case explanation: An Indian party sought appointment of an arbitrator in India relying on ancillary supply contracts, whereas the mother agreement designated Benin, West Africa as the seat of arbitration. The Supreme Court dismissed the Section 11 petition, holding that the foreign seat in the principal contract governs the composite transaction and excludes Part I jurisdiction.
Precedent chiefly relied on: PASL Wind Solutions Pvt. Ltd. v. GE Power Conversion India Pvt. Ltd. (2021) 7 SCC 1

Case name: Jagdeep Chowgule v. Sheela Chowgule
Issue in one line: Which court exercises jurisdiction over Section 29A(4) mandate extension and arbitrator substitution in a domestic family group arbitration seated in Goa.
Holding in one line: Applications under Section 29A(4) lie before the Principal Civil/Commercial Court of original jurisdiction at the arbitral seat under Section 2(1)(e), not a High Court lacking original civil jurisdiction.
Case explanation: In a dispute arising out of a Memorandum of Family Settlement of the Chowgule Group seated in Goa, a party approached the Bombay High Court at Goa for Section 29A extension while another approached the Commercial Court. In a reportable judgment, the Supreme Court held that even where the High Court appointed the arbitrator under Section 11, Section 29A(4) competence vests exclusively in the Principal Civil/Commercial Court at the seat under Section 2(1)(e).
Precedent chiefly relied on: Chief Engineer (NH) PWD (Roads) v. M/s BSC & C and C JV (2024)

Case name: J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. M/s Rash Builders India Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether conducting arbitral proceedings and signing the award in New Delhi shifts the express contractual seat from Srinagar.
Holding in one line: Once Srinagar is expressly fixed as the arbitral seat, conducting hearings or rendering the award in New Delhi for convenience does not shift supervisory jurisdiction from Srinagar.
Case explanation: Although the contract fixed Srinagar as the place of arbitration, the tribunal held sittings and signed the award in New Delhi for administrative convenience. The Supreme Court set aside the order entertaining post-award proceedings outside Srinagar, reiterating BGS SGS Soma and BBR (India) that convenient sittings under Section 20(3) never alter the juridical seat.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd. (2020) 4 SCC 234

Case name: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. v. M/s Bhel-pixel / GSCO Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
Issue in one line: Whether conducting arbitral hearings in Cuttack for administrative convenience shifts the seat from Sundargarh where the contract and work were anchored.
Holding in one line: Tribunal sittings held in Cuttack under Section 20(3) for convenience do not make Cuttack the seat; Section 34 challenges lie before the District Judge, Sundargarh.
Case explanation: In a mining contract anchored in Sundargarh district, Odisha, the sole arbitrator held sittings at Cuttack for convenience. When the award was challenged, a jurisdictional dispute arose between Cuttack and Sundargarh courts. The Supreme Court held that Cuttack was solely a Section 20(3) hearing venue and restored supervisory jurisdiction at Sundargarh.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BBR (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. S.P. Singla Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (2023) 1 SCC 693

Case name: Arcis Clean Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s Urja Global / Parshva Innovation
Issue in one line: Whether an exclusive Goa court jurisdiction clause coupled with Goa arbitration venue overrides Delhi where the agreement was executed.
Holding in one line: An exclusive Goa jurisdiction clause paired with Goa arbitration venue irrevocably fixes Goa as the juridical seat, ousting Delhi High Court jurisdiction.
Case explanation: Although the renewable energy agreement was signed in New Delhi, the dispute resolution clause stipulated arbitration in Goa and conferred exclusive jurisdiction on courts in Goa. The Supreme Court set aside the Delhi proceeding, holding that the coupling of a named venue (Goa) with an exclusive court jurisdiction clause (Goa) conclusively establishes Goa as the juridical seat.
Precedent chiefly relied on: BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd. (2020) 4 SCC 234
